name: EcoFlow 220W Bifacial Portable Solar Panel
summary: The best all-round folding panel: enough watts to matter, a stand that makes aiming easy, and a universal connector.
verdict: EcoFlow’s 220W bifacial panel is the folding panel we would recommend to most power station owners, whatever the brand. EcoFlow rates the front at 220W and the rear side for additional output from light reflected off the ground, and the carry case unfolds into a kickstand you can set to face the sun, which is where most of the real-world gain in portable solar comes from. Output is on MC4 connectors, the industry standard, and EcoFlow supplies a cable to its own XT60 input; other stations need their own MC4 adapter, which most include. At 220W it is the size that makes a meaningful dent in a 1kWh battery in a day without becoming too heavy for one person to carry and set up. The caveat is the bifacial claim: on dark soil or asphalt the back side adds little, and over sand, snow or a white tarp it adds more. Treat it as a bonus, not the headline.
skipIf: Bifacial gains depend heavily on the ground surface

name: Jackery SolarSaga 100W Solar Panel
summary: The easy choice for a Jackery Explorer, best bought in pairs for larger stations.
verdict: If you own a Jackery Explorer, the SolarSaga 100W is the low-friction choice. Jackery designs the cabling to plug into its stations, with adapters supplied for the different input sockets on older and newer Explorers, so there is very little to get wrong. The panel folds in half into a briefcase shape with a handle, has kickstands on the back so you can tilt it toward the sun, and adds USB ports for charging a phone straight off the panel. Its limitation is size. One 100W panel is a good match for a station of a few hundred watt-hours, but against a 1kWh-plus Explorer it will only put back a fraction of a charge on a good day; by the sun-hour math in this guide, expect something on the order of 300-400Wh from one panel on a clear summer day. For larger Explorers, buy two and connect them as Jackery’s manual describes, or look at our guide to the best Jackery power stations for bundled kits.

name: Anker SOLIX PS100 Portable Solar Panel
summary: A well-made, easy-to-carry 100W panel, ideal for small SOLIX stations and car camping.
verdict: Anker’s SOLIX PS100 is the compact 100W option for people who want one panel that folds small, sets up quickly and pairs neatly with a SOLIX power station. Anker builds in an adjustable kickstand so the panel can be tilted to suit the sun’s height, which matters most in spring, fall and winter, and lists high-efficiency monocrystalline cells. It is a natural partner for the smaller SOLIX stations, such as the C-series, where 100W of input is a sensible fraction of the battery and a decent day of sun can put back much of a charge. Against larger stations it is better thought of as one panel in a pair. Because Anker has sold several revisions and bundles under the PS100 name, check the listing for the exact output connector and its included cables, especially if your station is from another brand. Our guide to the best Anker SOLIX power stations covers which stations it suits best.

name: BLUETTI PV200 Solar Panel
summary: The 200W folding panel to buy if you want MC4 simplicity and might change station brands later.
verdict: BLUETTI’s PV200 is a good example of why MC4 output matters. It is a 200W folding panel that BLUETTI designs for its own stations, but because the output is the industry-standard MC4 connector, it works with nearly any station that ships with an MC4 adapter cable, which is most of them. BLUETTI lists monocrystalline cells with a high claimed efficiency, and the panel has kickstands on the back for tilting it toward the sun. At 200W, it is the size where a single panel starts to make real progress on a 1kWh battery: by the sun-hour arithmetic, a clear summer day could put back something like 500-800Wh with good aiming. The trade is footprint; unfolded, it needs a patch of ground, a truck bed or a picnic table. If you plan to wire two in series, add up their open-circuit voltage and compare it with your station’s limit first; that is where 200W panels most often catch people out.

name: EcoFlow 400W Portable Solar Panel
summary: The single-panel answer for a 1-2kWh station, provided your station’s input accepts its voltage.
verdict: The EcoFlow 400W is for people who want serious solar input without managing a pile of panels and branch cables. It is one folding panel, rated at 400W, with a case that becomes the kickstand and MC4 output with a cable for EcoFlow’s XT60 input. Paired with a 1-2kWh station such as an EcoFlow Delta, it is the setup most likely to refill the battery in a single good day: the sun-hour math suggests 1.2-1.6kWh from a clear summer day with careful aiming, before losses on cloudier days. Two points before you buy. First, it is big: unfolded, it covers a lot of ground and takes some effort to set up in wind. Second, a panel this size runs at a higher voltage than small 12V-class panels, which is good for efficiency but can exceed the input limit on small stations. Check the open-circuit voltage on the listing against your station’s manual, and do not buy it for a station with a modest solar input rating.

name: Renogy 100W Portable Solar Suitcase
summary: The right panel for charging a 12V RV, boat or camper battery; a fabric folder is better for power stations.
verdict: Renogy’s suitcase is a different kind of portable solar panel, and it is in this list for a different buyer. Two rigid panels hinge together in an aluminum frame with fold-out legs, and a charge controller is mounted on the back, with clips to connect straight to a 12V battery. That makes it a complete solar charging kit for an RV house battery, a trolling-motor battery or a van build, with no separate controller to buy. Renogy’s controllers support common battery chemistries, including lithium on current versions; check the listing for the exact controller and settings it ships with. For a portable power station, the built-in controller is extra hardware between the panel and a station that already has its own, so a fabric folding panel is usually the cleaner choice there. If your setup is built around a lithium RV battery, our guide to the best lithium RV batteries pairs well with this panel.

name: Goal Zero Boulder 100 Briefcase Solar Panel
summary: A panel built to live on a job site or truck bed, for buyers who value toughness over weight.
verdict: The Boulder 100 Briefcase is the panel you buy when the fabric folders feel too fragile. Goal Zero builds it as two monocrystalline panels behind tempered glass in an aluminum frame, hinged into a briefcase with a handle and a kickstand. It is meant to be thrown in a truck bed, left on a job site or set up on rocky ground without worrying about the panel surface, and Goal Zero designs Boulders to chain together when you need more input for a Yeti station. The cost is weight and price per watt: a glass-and-aluminum 100W panel is noticeably heavier than a fabric 100W folder, and it takes up more room in storage. For backpacking or anything carried far, it is the wrong choice. For a contractor running a Yeti on site, a ranch, or a family that stores its outage kit in a garage where things get knocked around, the durability is worth paying for. Check connector compatibility before pairing it with a non-Goal Zero station.

name: Goal Zero Nomad 20 Solar Panel
summary: Worth paying extra for if you own Goal Zero gear or want a panel you can stand up and aim properly.
verdict: Of all the panels here, the Nomad 20 is the one designed as part of a system. Goal Zero rates it at 20W and builds in a kickstand, which matters more than it seems: a panel tilted toward the sun produces noticeably more than one lying flat, and most fabric folders have to be hung or propped on whatever is at hand. Alongside the USB port for phones and banks, it carries an 8mm output that plugs into Goal Zero’s Sherpa power banks and small Yeti stations, and Nomads are designed to chain together when you need more input. That makes it the stepping stone if a small power station might follow your phone setup. The costs are weight and price; per watt it runs higher than a BigBlue or Anker. If a phone is all you will ever charge, the cheaper fabric panels do the same work. If you want a panel that stands up properly on a tailgate or a rock, choose this one.
